title: Young people are useful to society as heretics, not as good citizens
dek: College trains young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects, they just need permission.
why: Medium information density, but Amjad's path from chess to training models to building new Replit products is very concrete, useful for judging whether young people should start companies now.
who: Young people agonizing over whether to go to college or start a company now, plus founders, investors and anyone hiring, investing early-stage, or trying to understand how AI changes organizational forms.
skip: The sci-fi novel recap at the start, 0:00-2:04, can be skipped; go straight to the argument starting at 4:07.

points.h: Young people are useful as heretics
points.body: Amjad uses the sci-fi novel The City and the Stars as an analogy: in that city governed by an AGI, everyone is repeatedly reborn from compressed memories, until the machine breaks down and a genuinely new person is born, who immediately starts asking ‘what is outside the walls’. Amjad says the use of young people is to ask exactly this kind of question, to be heretics. But today's universities do the opposite — they tell you ‘we have already figured everything out, just learn our way’, and train you into a good citizen: marry, have kids, buy a house, buy a car. The problem is that world no longer exists; you can perform brilliantly in college and still end up unemployed with a pile of debt.

points.h: Silicon Valley is itself a monoculture
points.body: Amjad says every society has blind spots, and Silicon Valley has many too — it is a monoculture with a fixed way of thinking, so many ideas simply will not grow out of Silicon Valley. Even the most radical culture is, at bottom, a monoculture. So you need young people to experiment, to attempt what is considered impossible, and occasionally someone breaks through: impossible yesterday, suddenly possible today because the technology changed. What college should do is gather people with clear minds and first-principles thinking, and encourage them to question what is deeply believed.

points.h: Raising at 18 is an overused option
points.body: Gagan says young people today face a deeply unfair binary: either go to a four-year college and be managed by attendance, homework, exams and grades; or tomorrow someone hands you $50,000 to start a company. He thinks the investor path should be used far less, and only a very small number of teenagers should raise money. Most people at 17 or 18 know they want to enter the business world, but having two years to explore and learn without pressure is precious. He argues for a middle ground: two years to explore freely, with Silicon Valley actively sending information and resources your way, and more support if you have a good idea.

points.h: Starting too early is premature optimization
points.body: Amjad borrows a phrase from programming, ‘premature optimization is the root of all evil’: a lot of founding is premature optimization. He sees many kids now inside a circle where friends are raising big rounds, some became unicorns, so the motivation becomes a negative one like envy, and then they pre-commit to an idea they are not even interested in, optimizing early for a path they have not yet reached. He says the real question is what your curiosity is driving you toward; once you find the idea you are willing to spend ten years, a lifetime on, it has enormous gravity, you cannot escape it — he himself actively did not want to start a company, but the thing blew up into a startup on its own. He also says VCs now go to Stanford and give students a million dollars with no idea yet, and the moment they start there is already a cap table, which is a bit like the music industry signing young artists.

points.h: From chess all the way to training models
points.body: Amjad says he has always oscillated between ‘wanting to build things’ and ‘wanting to read and explore widely’, the two feed each other, a recursive process. He gives his recent obsession with chess as an example: he started playing very late, does not know why he was interested, then started writing programs to solve chess, training models, and found that LLMs are terrible at chess and hallucinate moves that do not exist. To figure it out, he had never trained a model, yet spent a lot of time studying how to train one. He realized from this that AI can now do machine learning itself, just as in 2024 Replit's agent suddenly could write code and afterward coding completely changed, machine learning may be at that same moment — he calls it vibe research or auto research. He is now building products at Replit to let anyone become a machine learning researcher, or let a boss with data fine-tune a model to solve a specific problem.

Amjad thinks the form of the company will change. Silicon Valley has tried many experiments to remake companies — Holacracy, Medium tried it, GitHub tried a no-manager system, all failed spectacularly, but he thinks that was a technology problem: now you can let agents act as the glue in an organization, turn bureaucratic processes into invisible things machines do in the background, while people get real autonomy to do what interests them most, and AI can even judge your impact. He says he has already changed how management works at Replit, calls it a ‘self-driving company’, and ultimately the company will run itself. He admits he does not have a fully formed idea, but is very sure everything will change, and much faster than you think; if you do not natively understand this stuff, the transition will be hard.

points.h: Trust makes money arrive six weeks faster
points.body: Gagan says he volunteers in local politics in his spare time, and the biggest takeaway is understanding how valuable trust is. He gives a concrete comparison: in a nonprofit, after a donor verbally commits $50,000 to you, the probability that the money actually lands in your account is only about 20% to 50%; in Silicon Valley, that probability is about 75% to 100%. The difference is that if you are certain the money is coming, you can confidently push forward, and by the time the check actually arrives you have already advanced six weeks, which makes the check even more valuable. Conversely, without trust you change your approach out of fear the donor will be unhappy, drift from your mission, and are left with only anxiety and stress. He thinks this can be transplanted into schools: trust students to do what they want to do.

points.h: No grades means no fulcrum to push against
points.body: Asked how to handle disruptive students — like Zuckerberg, who built FaceMash and nearly got expelled — Gagan says there must of course be red lines, sexual harassment, publicly humiliating others and the like need rules, and you need to build trust and a positive-sum atmosphere. But he says one core principle of the academy sidesteps the problem entirely: no grades, no exams, so the resistance students have to push against is already much smaller. So if you want to build FaceMash, go build it, and he is willing to defend that right even if he personally finds the idea weird and does not like it. He thinks that as long as you create an environment of trust and do not let students develop an anti-authority mindset, you can unlock a huge amount of creativity and opportunity. Amjad adds that this drive to test boundaries can be channeled in a healthy direction: kids who learn to code and hack on Roblox, rather than being sent to prison, could be given a sandbox, their talent discovered, and then directed into cybersecurity jobs or even government.

Amjad's name for AI doing machine learning research itself, by analogy with vibe coding.
The Aristotelian ethical view: act in a way you would not be ashamed of whether or not anyone is watching.
